Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — SonicWall SMA Zero-Days Exploited Before Disclosure to Gain Root Access
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

New wp2shell WordPress Core Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 6 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Updated July 18, 2026: the two flaws now carry CVE IDs, the full mechanism has been published, a persistent-object-cache condition has surfaced, and a working proof-of-concept is public. The story below reflects all of it. An anonymous HTTP request can run code on a WordPress site. The bug is in core, so a bare install with zero plugins is exploitable. Every 6.9 and 7.0 site was in range until

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated request to WordPress REST batch/v1 endpoint (wp2shell CVE-2026-63030) · [LLM] Successful (HTTP 200) response from WordPress batch/v1 to an anonymous caller
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] WordPress web-server / PHP-FPM process spawns a shell interpreter · [LLM] PHP webshell written under wp-content by WordPress web process
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] wp-config.php read via shell utility (post-RCE DB credential theft)
Unauthenticated request to WordPress REST batch/v1 endpoint (wp2shell CVE-2026-63030) AIExploitation High
Hunts anonymous HTTP requests to the WordPress core batch endpoint on both reachable forms (/wp-json/batch/v1 and the always-on /?rest_route=/batch/v1), which is the single entry point for the wp2shell pre-auth RCE. Flags callers with no WordPress auth cookie, and boosts confidence when the SQLi sink parameter author__not_in appears. Rationale: Anchors on the two concrete endpoint forms the researchers state are BOTH reachable (/wp-json/batch/v1 and /?rest_route=/batch/v1) plus the author__not_in SQLi parameter confirmed by Searchlight/Hadrian as the CVE-2026-60137 sink; the WP auth-cookie absence encodes the article's 'anonymous user' precondition. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://hadrian.io/blog/wp2shell-a-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-cores-rest-batch-api • https://nebula.design/security/wp2shell-wordpress-rce/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/wp2shell-rce-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate plugins/mobile apps (e.g. block editor, headless front-ends, Jetpack) that batch REST calls via /wp-json/batch/v1
  • Site health / uptime monitors probing REST endpoints
  • Authenticated admin actions where the cookie parse failed to be logged by the proxy
  • Security scanners (WPScan, Nessus) run by the site's own team
  • CDN health checks hitting rest_route
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<uptime-monitor-ip>") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "jetpack" and Url has "author__not_in"   // tighten to the SQLi-sink variant to strip benign batch traffic
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP to /batch/v1 in the last 24h; check for author__not_in, POST bodies, and whether any returned HTTP 200. Confirm the target's WordPress version is in 6.9.0-6.9.4 or 7.0.0-7.0.1. 2) Contain: at the WAF block BOTH /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 (query-string route included), and force-update the site to 7.0.2/6.9.5. 3) Hunt: pivot to the web host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells, new .php files under wp-content/uploads, and outbound connections from the web user in the minutes after the batch request.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "/wp-json/batch/v1" or Url has "rest_route=/batch/v1" or Url has "rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1"
| where HttpMethod == "POST" or Url has "author__not_in"
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderCookie) or HttpRequestHeaderCookie !has "wordpress_logged_in_"   // anonymous caller = no WP auth cookie
| extend SqliSink = iff(Url has "author__not_in", "author__not_in", "")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, SqliSink, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: WordPress wp2shell REST batch/v1 Endpoint Access (CVE-2026-63030)

description: Detects HTTP requests to the WordPress core REST batch endpoint on both reachable path forms, the entry point for the wp2shell pre-auth RCE chain.

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/wp-json/batch/v1'
  selection_route:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'rest_route=/batch/v1'

WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/wp-json/batch/v1*" OR Web.url="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.url="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.url, Web.uri_query, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval sqli_indicator=if(match(url."author__not_in") OR match(uri_query,"author__not_in"),"yes","no") | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/wp-json/batch/v1*" OR Web.url="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.url="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=/batch/v1*" OR Web.uri_query="*rest_route=%2Fbatch%2Fv1*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_method, Web.url, Web.uri_query, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval sqli_indicator=if(match(url."author__not_in") OR match(uri_query,"author__not_in"),"yes","no") | sort - lastTime
Successful (HTTP 200) response from WordPress batch/v1 to an anonymous caller AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces sources that receive an HTTP 200 from the WordPress batch endpoint without ever presenting a WordPress authentication cookie — the observable signature of successful wp2shell exploitation, since the article notes '200 traffic against batch/v1 will show when the attackers arrive.' Aggregates by source to distinguish single-shot exploitation from noise. Rationale: Uses the article's own detection thesis — a 200 on batch/v1 is the arrival signal — combined with the anonymous-caller (no wordpress_logged_in_ cookie) condition to separate successful anonymous exploitation from authenticated legitimate batch use. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://hadrian.io/blog/wp2shell-a-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-cores-rest-batch-api
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Headless/decoupled WordPress front-ends that legitimately call batch/v1 anonymously for public content
  • Public REST batch reads that don't require auth (e.g. published posts)
  • Proxy stripped the cookie header before logging, mislabeling an authenticated user as anonymous
  • Load balancer synthetic 200 health checks
  • Cached 200 responses served by a CDN in front of WordPress
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-headless-frontend-ip>") and DstHostname !in ("<staging-host>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged source, order its batch/v1 requests by time and inspect the request just before the first 200 for author__not_in or batch sub-request arrays; confirm site version is affected. 2) Contain: block both batch routes at the WAF and force-patch to 7.0.2/6.9.5; snapshot the web host for forensics before it is cleaned. 3) Hunt: correlate the 200 timestamp with host telemetry — php-fpm/apache child shells, new webshell files, wp-config.php reads by shell utilities.

WordPress web-server / PHP-FPM process spawns a shell interpreter AIInstallation High
Detects the WordPress runtime user (apache2/httpd/nginx/php-fpm/php) spawning an interactive shell or scripting interpreter — the execution stage that follows successful wp2shell RCE, where 'run code' becomes a real shell. High fidelity because the web-server runtime should never fork /bin/sh, python, or netcat during normal request handling. Rationale: Web-server/PHP runtimes never legitimately fork interactive shells during request handling; pairing the specific WordPress web users (php-fpm/apache/nginx) as parent with shell/interpreter children is the classic post-RCE execution signal for the article's 'run code' outcome. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://cyberinsider.com/wordpress-releases-emergency-update-for-critical-wp2shell-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress plugins shelling out (e.g. image processing via ImageMagick/exec, backup plugins calling mysqldump)
  • WP-CLI cron jobs run under the web user
  • Deployment/CI scripts that run as www-data
  • Server monitoring agents invoked by php-fpm
  • Composer or wp-cli update tasks triggered from the admin panel
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","wp cron","mysqldump","convert","imagemagick"))   // strip known plugin/cli shell-outs
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child process command line and its own children; a reverse-shell (nc/socat/bash -i /dev/tcp) or interpreter one-liner is a confirmed compromise. Check the parent php-fpm's recent HTTP context for batch/v1 hits. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, kill the shell process tree, and rotate DB and WordPress secret keys (wp-config salts). 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web user in the last 24h (webshells under wp-content), new cron entries, and outbound C2 from the shell.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","php7.4","php8.0","php8.1","php8.2","php8.3")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

PHP webshell written under wp-content by WordPress web process AIInstallation High
Alerts when the WordPress runtime user creates an executable PHP file (.php/.phtml/.php5/.phar) inside wp-content/uploads, /plugins or /themes — the persistence step where wp2shell RCE drops a backdoor. The uploads directory in particular should never receive server-side executable PHP. Rationale: wp-content/uploads is a data directory that legitimately never receives server-generated executable PHP; a web-user-owned .php write there (or into plugins/themes) is a textbook webshell-drop and directly maps the RCE to persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/wp2shell-rce-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Plugin/theme install or auto-update writing legitimate PHP into wp-content/plugins or /themes
  • Caching plugins (WP Super Cache, W3TC) generating advanced-cache.php or cache PHP files
  • Backup/staging plugins restoring a site into wp-content
  • Page-builder plugins compiling PHP templates
  • Developer manually deploying a plugin via SFTP as the web user
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/wp-content/plugins/" and (FileName has "cache" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "wp-cli"))   // exclude cache-plugin and wp-cli plugin installs
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the new file's first bytes — eval/base64_decode/assert/system/$_POST/$_GET patterns confirm a webshell; note whether it landed in uploads (near-certain malicious) vs plugins (check against a known plugin update). 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the batch routes, isolate the host, and reset WordPress salts + DB creds. 3) Hunt: search access logs for GET/POST to the dropped filename (attacker interaction), and look for sibling drops and web-user shell spawns around the same timestamp.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","php7.4","php8.0","php8.1","php8.2","php8.3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| sort by TimeGenerated desc

wp-config.php read via shell utility (post-RCE DB credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects non-runtime processes (cat, grep, tar, curl, base64, php -r, etc.) accessing wp-config.php by command line — the credential-access move after wp2shell RCE, where the attacker exfiltrates the WordPress DB credentials and secret keys stored in that file. Excludes the normal per-request reads php-fpm/apache perform. Rationale: Framing wp-config.php access via shell/exfil utilities (not the php-fpm runtime, which reads it every request) isolates the attacker's DB-credential-theft action; wp-config.php holds the DB user/password and auth salts that follow-on lateral movement needs. Cross-checked against: • https://hadrian.io/blog/wp2shell-a-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-cores-rest-batch-api • https://nebula.design/security/wp2shell-wordpress-rce/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually inspecting wp-config.php during troubleshooting
  • Backup jobs that tar/gzip the WordPress root including wp-config.php
  • Migration/staging tooling copying wp-config.php between environments
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Puppet) reading the file to template values
  • Developer grepping for a DB constant during debugging
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cron","ansible","puppet","backup") and not (ProcessCommandLine has "tar" and ProcessCommandLine has "backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the acting user and parent process — if the parent traces to a php-fpm/apache child shell or an unexpected session, treat as confirmed theft; benign hits trace to an admin's interactive login. 2) Contain: rotate the WordPress DB credentials and all wp-config salts/keys immediately, and restrict DB access to the app host; isolate if RCE is confirmed. 3) Hunt: check for outbound transfer of the file (curl/scp/base64 piped to a socket), DB dumps (mysqldump), and reuse of the DB creds from other hosts.

| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "wp-config.php"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","less","more","head","tail","tar","cp","curl","wget","base64","xxd","strings","php","zip","gzip","scp","nc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "wp-config.php"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cat","grep","egrep","less","more","head","tail","tar","cp","curl","wget","base64","xxd","strings","php","zip","gzip","scp","nc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

WordPress wp2shell batch REST API pre-auth RCE exploitation (CVE-2026-63030/60137) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the WordPress core REST batch endpoint /wp-json/batch/v1 (or rest_route=/batch/v1) that carry the batch-route-confusion + author_exclude/author__not_in SQL injection used by the wp2shell pre-auth RCE. Article-specific: anchors on the exact entry-point path plus the injected SQLi parameter and time-based payload tokens. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim article/PoC strings: entry path /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 (Code Block 1/2) plus the SQLi injection parameter author_exclude/author__not_in and time-based SLEEP() payload confirmed by the Searchlight write-up and the public detection PoC. Endpoint + non-GET method + SQLi token is very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://github.com/Senanfurkan/wordpress-cve-2026-63030 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-63030/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-party plugins/mobile apps that batch REST calls through /wp-json/batch/v1 (no SQLi tokens present, so the SQLi selection filters them)
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Nessus/wp2shell.com checker) probing the batch route from known scanner IPs
  • Security researchers or the site owner testing exposure with the published PoC
  • WAF/CDN health checks that touch REST routes but not the batch endpoint with injection params
Suppression filter
| where not (src IN ("10.0.0.0/8") AND like(user_agent,"%HealthCheck%"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests to /batch/v1 from the source IP over the prior 24h; check scStatus (200 with post-shaped response body indicates the route-confusion succeeded) and confirm the target WordPress version is < 6.9.5 / < 7.0.2. 2) Contain: block /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 at the WAF/CDN, force the site to 7.0.2 (or 6.9.5), and rotate DB credentials if injection returned data. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host — look for web-daemon-spawned shells and newly written .php files under wp-content/ within minutes of the request.

| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=cIP, Method=csMethod, UriStem=csUriStem, UriQuery=csUriQuery, Status=scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent, Site=sSiteName),

Web server daemon (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) spawning a shell or network tool — wp2shell post-exploit code execution AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation stage of the wp2shell RCE: a WordPress web worker (php-fpm, apache2/httpd, nginx, or IIS w3wp/php-cgi) spawning an interactive shell or egress tool (sh/bash, nc/ncat, curl/wget, python/perl, cmd/powershell). Article-specific because the flaw yields arbitrary code execution under the web user with no plugin involved. Rationale: Article states the flaw 'chains into remote code execution' against a stock install under the web user; the highest-fidelity host signal for that is a WordPress web daemon (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) parenting a shell or egress binary — a parent+child pairing that is abnormal for a web server. Parent set is WordPress-specific, not a generic LOLBin template. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress plugins that legitimately call exec()/shell_exec() (e.g. image optimizers invoking convert, backup plugins invoking mysqldump/tar)
  • WP-Cron or deploy hooks running via php-fpm that shell out to curl/wget for remote fetches
  • Server management panels (Plesk/cPanel) whose PHP workers spawn shells for admin tasks
  • CI/CD or WP-CLI automation executed under the web account during scheduled maintenance
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i","bash -c","sh -c","-e /bin","base64 -d","|sh","| sh","IEX","-nop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for reverse-shell/download syntax (/dev/tcp, nc -e, bash -i, curl|sh) and correlate the timestamp against UC1 batch-endpoint hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending php-fpm/worker child tree, and pull the box out of the load balancer. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by that PID (UC3) and outbound connections from the web daemon; capture bash history and /tmp for staged payloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProc=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","perl","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New PHP file written into WordPress web root by a web daemon — wp2shell web shell drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunts web shell persistence following the wp2shell RCE: a WordPress web worker (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp/php-cgi) creating a new .php/.phtml/.php5/.phar file under wp-content, wp-admin, or wp-includes. Article-specific because unauthenticated RCE in core is routinely followed by dropping an attacker PHP payload into the web-accessible tree. Rationale: WordPress web daemons should not author new PHP files in the web root outside of an update; pairing the web-worker writer (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) with a fresh .php under wp-content/wp-admin/wp-includes is a high-signal web shell drop for a core RCE that runs as the web user. Web-root paths are WordPress-specific, not a generic file-write template. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.cryptika.com/new-wp2shell-rce-vulnerability-hits-millions-of-wordpress-sites-emergency-patch-released/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress core auto-update to 6.9.5/7.0.2 rewriting bundled PHP files (expected right now given forced auto-updates)
  • Plugin/theme installation or update from the admin dashboard writing PHP into wp-content/plugins or /themes
  • Caching plugins (WP Super Cache/W3 Total Cache) generating advanced-cache.php or object-cache.php drop-ins
  • Backup/restore or staging-sync tooling repopulating the web root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "wp-cron" and FolderPath !has "cache" and not (FileName in~ ("object-cache.php","advanced-cache.php","db.php"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the created file — flag short files containing eval/base64_decode/system/assert/$_REQUEST/$_POST/preg_replace(/e); compare the writer PID and timestamp against UC1 batch-endpoint requests and known update windows. 2) Contain: quarantine the file (do not delete before imaging), block web access to it, and isolate the host if the content is a shell. 3) Hunt: enumerate all files touched by the same PID/session, review access logs for GET/POST hits on the new filename, and check for scheduled tasks or wp_options/wp_users tampering.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/","\\wp-content\\","/wp-admin/","\\wp-admin\\","/wp-includes/","\\wp-includes\\")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7" or FileName endswith ".phar"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, WebDaemon=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/wp-content/","\\wp-content\\","/wp-admin/","\\wp-admin\\","/wp-includes/","\\wp-includes\\")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","php5","php7","phar")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenSSL HollowByte Flaw Could Freeze Server Memory with 11-Byte TLS Requests

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 3 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

Eleven bytes will make an unpatched OpenSSL server set aside up to 131 KB of memory for a message that never arrives. On the glibc systems Okta tested, that memory is gone until the process restarts. OpenSSL shipped the HollowByte fix in June with no CVE, no advisory, and no changelog entry pointing at it. Okta's Red Team, which reported the denial-of-service bug and named it, published the

Unpatched OpenSSL exposed to HollowByte DoS (pre-2026-06-09 build, no CVE to scan) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces OpenSSL installs on branches 3.0/3.4/3.5/3.6/4.0 below the 2026-06-09 fixed releases (3.0.21, 3.4.6, 3.5.7, 3.6.3, 4.0.1) that carry the un-numbered HollowByte TLS length-over-allocation DoS. Because HollowByte shipped with NO CVE/advisory, normal scanners miss it; this hunt keys on the raw version and on CVE-2026-34183 (the QUIC PATH_CHALLENGE DoS that shipped in the SAME June 9 train) as a proxy for a build that predates the fix. Rationale: Uses the exact fixed-release list from the article (3.0.21/3.4.6/3.5.7/3.6.3/4.0.1, dated 2026-06-09) and CVE-2026-34183 as a same-train proxy for a pre-fix build. Corroborated that CVE-2026-34183 shipped 2026-06-09 and affects 3.0/3.4/3.5/3.6/4.0 (not 1.1.1/1.0.2) via Red Hat Bugzilla and openssl-library.org, so 1.x is deliberately excluded to avoid FPs on branches whose HollowByte status is unconfirmed. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.okta.com/articles/2026/06/openssl-hollowbtye-a-dos-hiding-in-11-bytes/ • https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2481885 • https://openssl-library.org/news/vulnerabilities/ • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/06/09/15
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro-backported package (Red Hat/Debian) that reports the old base version string but already contains the patch — the article explicitly warns version reporting lies after a backport
  • OpenSSL statically linked into an appliance/container image where TVM reads the wrapper version, not the linked libssl
  • Build patched for CVE-2026-34183 but where the maintainer took the QUIC fix only and not the HollowByte TLS commit (rare, but the reason the Defender version-hunt exists alongside the CVE proxy)
  • Development / test hosts intentionally pinned to an old OpenSSL for compatibility testing
  • 4.0.1 hosts still exposed via the un-fixed DTLS path — these will NOT appear in this hunt because the TLS branch is patched
Suppression filter
| where EndOfSupportStatus != "EOS" or isempty(EndOfSupportStatus)  // optional: focus on supported builds where a backport is plausible
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm whether the host actually terminates TLS/DTLS on an internet-facing port (nginx/haproxy/httpd/stunnel) — an unlinked or loopback-only OpenSSL is low priority; check the package changelog or ask the maintainer whether they rebased on the 2026-06-09 release or cherry-picked PR 30792/30793/30794. 2) Contain: for internet-facing terminators, upgrade to the listed fixed release and restart the service (buffer only frees on process restart); if immediate patch is impossible, front the service with a proxy that fully buffers/validates the ClientHello before backend hand-off. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'OpenSSL TLS server OOM/memory-pressure' on the same hosts to see whether exploitation is already underway, and enumerate sibling hosts sharing the same golden image or package pin.
// Direct build-version hunt — catches HollowByte-vulnerable OpenSSL even where the CVE-2026-34183 proxy is patched but the un-numbered fix was not backported.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareVendor has "openssl" or SoftwareName has "openssl"
| extend Parts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1]), Patch = toint(Parts[2])
| where (Major == 3 and Minor == 0 and Patch < 21)   // 3.0.x fixed at 3.0.21
     or (Major == 3 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 6)    // 3.4.x fixed at 3.4.6
     or (Major == 3 and Minor == 5 and Patch < 7)    // 3.5.x fixed at 3.5.7
     or (Major == 3 and Minor == 6 and Patch < 3)    // 3.6.x fixed at 3.6.3
     or (Major == 4 and Minor == 0 and Patch < 1)    // 4.0.x fixed at 4.0.1
     or (Major == 3 and Minor in (1, 2, 3))          // EOL 3.x branches, no HollowByte fix shipped
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, EndOfSupportStatus
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc
// Proxy hunt: TVM still flags this OpenSSL for CVE-2026-34183 (shipped in the same 2026-06-09 release as the un-numbered HollowByte fix) => build predates the fix => also HollowByte-vulnerable.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "openssl"
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-34183"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-34183" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-34183" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
OpenSSL TLS server OOM-kill / memory pressure (HollowByte glibc heap fragmentation) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the HollowByte impact signature: an OpenSSL-linked TLS-terminating server (nginx, httpd/apache2, haproxy, stunnel) killed by the Linux OOM-killer or emitting OOM/oom_reaper events. HollowByte's distinguishing trait is that freed buffers never return to the kernel on glibc, so RSS climbs and stays climbed until the process is OOM-killed — without ever crossing a connection ceiling. Rationale: Keys on the article's/Okta's stated impact: glibc keeps freed small/medium chunks so RSS 'stays climbed long after the attacker has gone' and the server is 'OOM-killed' (nginx named explicitly). The kernel OOM-killer line ('Out of memory: Killed process N (nginx)') plus a TLS-terminator process name is high-fidelity and article-specific. Defender AH has no OOM ActionType for Linux, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; the signal lives in kernel syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.okta.com/articles/2026/06/openssl-hollowbtye-a-dos-hiding-in-11-bytes/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hollowbyte-ddos-flaw-bloats-openssl-server-memory-with-11-byte-payload/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1499.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuinely undersized VM where nginx/haproxy is OOM-killed under legitimate peak traffic, not attack
  • A memory leak in a web-app module (PHP-FPM, mod_php) rather than in OpenSSL's handshake buffers
  • cgroup/container memory-limit kills (memory.max) on a co-located sidecar that names the TLS process incidentally
  • Batch/cron jobs on the same host spiking memory and triggering global OOM that reaps the web server as the largest RSS consumer
  • Kubernetes eviction storms that surface as OOM messages referencing the ingress-nginx pod
Suppression filter
| where SampleMessage !has "memory.max" and SampleMessage !has "cgroup"  // drop container memory-limit kills; keep global/host OOM which matches the HollowByte host-exhaustion pattern
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the OOM victim is an internet-facing TLS terminator and correlate the kill timestamps with a rising RSS trend on that PID (node_exporter/process metrics) and with source-IP diversity of half-open/never-completed TLS connections at the LB — HollowByte holds workers on bodies that never arrive. 2) Contain: restart the affected service to reclaim the frozen glibc arenas (memory only returns on process restart), then patch OpenSSL to the 2026-06-09 fixed release (3.0.21/3.4.6/3.5.7/3.6.3/4.0.1) and, as a stopgap, set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX / front with a fully-buffering proxy and lower handshake timeouts. 3) Hunt: run UC 'Unpatched OpenSSL exposed to HollowByte' across the fleet to find every host on a pre-fix build, and review perimeter logs for sources opening many TLS connections that send only a tiny ClientHello then go silent.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Facility in ("kern", "syslog", "daemon")
| where SyslogMessage has "Out of memory" or SyslogMessage has "oom-kill" or SyslogMessage has "oom_reaper"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("nginx", "openssl", "httpd", "apache2", "haproxy", "stunnel")
| summarize KillCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostName, Facility
| where KillCount >= 2   // 2 = repeated OOM of a TLS terminator within the window; single OOMs are common one-offs
| sort by KillCount desc
title: OpenSSL TLS Server Killed by Linux OOM-Killer (HollowByte Memory Exhaustion)

Seven Malicious Vite npm Packages Use Blockchain C2 to Deliver a RAT

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a cluster of seven malicious npm packages targeting the Vite frontend tooling ecosystem as part of a software supply chain attack. The malicious package campaign, codenamed ViteVenom by Checkmarx, marks an expansion of ChainVeil, which was observed using an "unprecedented" four-tier blockchain-based command-and-control (C2) infrastructure spanning Tron,

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ViteVenom malicious npm package install/presence (@vitejs typosquat cluster) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node/build process spawning interactive shell (ViteVenom RAT reverse shell) · [LLM] Shell profile persistence (.bashrc/.zshrc/.profile) modified by node/npm
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node/build process egress to blockchain RPC & explorer infra (Tron/BSC/Aptos C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
ViteVenom malicious npm package install/presence (@vitejs typosquat cluster) AIDelivery High
Hunts installation or on-disk presence of the seven named ViteVenom scoped npm packages that impersonate the @vitejs/* namespace. Article-specific: matches the exact package specifiers, not a generic 'suspicious npm install' template. Rationale: Uses the seven exact scoped package specifiers named in the article as install-cmdline and node_modules on-disk anchors; these strings are unique to the campaign so FP risk is minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html • https://www.guardianmssp.com/2026/07/17/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use-blockchain-c2-to-deliver-a-rat/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally pulling the IOC packages into a sandbox for analysis
  • Internal dependency-audit tooling referencing the package names in scan output/logs (matches cmdline substring)
  • A legitimately named future @vitejs package coincidentally sharing a similar path fragment (unlikely given exact-string match)
  • Threat-intel enrichment scripts echoing the package names on the command line
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-analysis","detonate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: On the alerting host, confirm the package exists under node_modules/@<scope>/<name> and inspect package.json main/module entry and any loader JS for blockchain RPC calls. Identify the developer/user and project. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill node processes, delete the package and lockfile entries, and rotate ALL credentials that were reachable from that dev environment (npm tokens, cloud keys, SSH). 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC2/UC3/UC4 on the same host+user — blockchain egress, node-spawned shells, and .bashrc/.zshrc/.profile edits — to confirm RAT delivery and persistence.
let Packages = dynamic(["@uw010010/vite-tree","@vite-tab/tab","@vite-ln/build-ts","@vite-mcp/vite-type","@vite-pro/vite-ui","@vitets/vite-ts","@vite-ts/vite-ui"]);
let InstallCmd = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","npm-cli.js","pnpm","pnpm.exe","yarn","yarn.exe","node","node.exe") or FileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","pnpm","yarn")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (Packages)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath;
let OnDisk = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" and FolderPath has_any (Packages)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union InstallCmd, OnDisk
| order by Timestamp desc
let Packages = dynamic(["@uw010010/vite-tree","@vite-tab/tab","@vite-ln/build-ts","@vite-mcp/vite-type","@vite-pro/vite-ui","@vitets/vite-ts","@vite-ts/vite-ui"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","node") or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (Packages)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine

Node/build process egress to blockchain RPC & explorer infra (Tron/BSC/Aptos C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts a node/npm/dev-build process contacting Tron, Binance Smart Chain, or Aptos RPC/explorer endpoints — the ViteVenom loader's blockchain-based payload-pointer retrieval. Article-specific: a frontend build tool has no business querying trongrid/bscscan/aptos fullnodes. Rationale: Article states the loader queries Tron for the latest attacker-wallet tx, decodes it to a BSC tx hash, then pulls the encrypted payload from BSC input (Aptos as fallback); scoping to the public RPC/explorer domains of exactly those three chains AND a node/build parent is the campaign's C2 signature. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html • https://tronscan.org/ • https://bscscan.com/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1104
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/dApp developer whose project genuinely integrates Tron/BSC/Aptos SDKs and calls these RPCs from node during dev
  • Crypto-analytics or wallet tooling installed on the same workstation
  • CI runner building a blockchain-adjacent project that resolves bscscan/aptos APIs
  • Browser-based blockchain explorer usage misattributed if process attribution is weak
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("web3","tronweb","@aptos-labs","ethers","hardhat","truffle")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the initiating node process's working directory/project — is this a legitimate web3 project or a standard frontend app? A plain Vite/React app calling trongrid is highly suspicious. Capture the RemoteIP and full URL path. 2) Contain: Block the blockchain infra egress for non-web3 dev hosts, isolate the host, and capture node process memory before killing. 3) Hunt: Check for the direct-HTTP C2 fallback (non-blockchain outbound from the same node PID), UC1 package presence, and UC4 shell-profile persistence on the host.
let ChainInfra = dynamic(["trongrid.io","tronscan.org","tronscanapi.com","bscscan.com","bsc-dataseed","bnbchain.org","aptoslabs.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","npm","pnpm","yarn","vite","esbuild")
| where RemoteUrl has_any (ChainInfra) or RemoteUrl endswith "aptoslabs.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let ChainInfra = dynamic(["trongrid.io","tronscan.org","tronscanapi.com","bscscan.com","bsc-dataseed","bnbchain.org","aptoslabs.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (ChainInfra)
| join kind=leftouter (ImProcessCreate | where ActingProcessName has "node" | project DvcHostname, ActorUsername) on DvcHostname
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, ActorUsername

Node/build process spawning interactive shell (ViteVenom RAT reverse shell) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a node/npm/vite build process spawning bash/sh/zsh/powershell/cmd — consistent with the ViteVenom RAT's reverse-shell capability launched from the import-time loader. Article-specific: pairs the supply-chain parent (node) with unexpected shell children. Rationale: Article says the delivered RAT provides a reverse shell launched at import time from the loader; node/vite spawning a shell interpreter is the execution-layer manifestation and pairs the supply-chain parent with the shell child for fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm/yarn lifecycle scripts legitimately invoking sh -c during install/build (very common)
  • Build tooling shelling out to git, rimraf, or shell wrappers
  • Developer running package.json scripts that call bash helpers
  • Monorepo task runners (nx, turbo) spawning shells via node
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-i","/dev/tcp","bash -i"," nc ","|sh","curl","wget") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(reverse|socket|/dev/tcp)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect the shell child's command line — benign lifecycle shells run known build commands (git, rm, cp); a reverse-shell child will have socket/redirection (/dev/tcp, bash -i, nc, curl|sh) or connect outbound. Correlate to UC2 blockchain egress on the same host/time. 2) Contain: Kill the process tree, isolate the host, snapshot memory. 3) Hunt: Enumerate the responsible project's dependencies against the UC1 IOC list and check .bashrc/.zshrc/.profile (UC4) for persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","npm","pnpm","yarn","vite")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","powershell.exe","pwsh","cmd.exe")
