GoSerpent staged-data exfiltration to network shared drives via TmcPayload/ThumbcacheService AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GoSerpent exfiltration step where collected/archived data is moved out through network shared drives. Fires when a named collection/exfil tool (TmcLoader, TmcPayload, ThumbcacheService, McMx, Stowaway) writes to a UNC (\\host\share) path — the article's described exfil-via-network-share behaviour. Rationale: Kaspersky states the actor exfiltrates collected data 'through network shared drives' with TmcLoader/TmcPayload after ThumbcacheService collection; anchoring the named tools writing to a UNC path targets that exfil hop specifically rather than generic SMB writes. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1041 T1039
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/sync agents writing to a file-server share (but not under these tool names)
  • Admin copying archives to a departmental share
  • DFS replication touching UNC paths
  • A benign tool coincidentally named with a 'Tmc'/'Stowaway' string writing to shares
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the destination share and files written; identify whether the source host was recently seen running ThumbcacheService/7-Zip collection. 2) Contain: revoke the writing account's access to the target share, isolate the source host, snapshot the destination share for scoping. 3) Hunt: follow the share to the next hop — which other hosts read the staged archive — and check egress from that host to external C2 to complete the exfil chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","ThumbcacheService","McMx","Stowaway")
| where FolderPath startswith @"\\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, ShareName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","ThumbcacheService","McMx","Stowaway")
| where TargetFilePath startswith @"\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
title: GoSerpent Toolset Writing to Network Share (Exfil Staging)
id: 8e0f5c2d-7a49-4b31-9f18-3c6d1b2e4409
description: Detects GoSerpent-named tools writing files to a UNC network share path, consistent with exfiltration via network shared drives.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-goserpent-malware-targets-southeast.html
  - https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.t1039
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|contains:
      - 'TmcLoader'
      - 'TmcPayload'
      - 'ThumbcacheService'
      - 'McMx'
      - 'Stowaway'
    TargetFilename|startswith: '\\'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\TmcLoader* OR *\\TmcPayload* OR *\\ThumbcacheService* OR *\\McMx* OR *\\Stowaway* OR *\\tmcpayload*) @TargetFilename:\\\\*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/(TmcLoader|TmcPayload|ThumbcacheService|McMx|Stowaway)/i
| TargetFileName=/^\\\\/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("TmcLoader.exe","TmcPayload.exe","McMx.exe","Stowaway.exe") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("TmcLoader.exe","TmcPayload.exe")) Processes.process="*\\\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("TmcLoader.exe","TmcPayload.exe","McMx.exe","Stowaway.exe") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("TmcLoader.exe","TmcPayload.exe")) Processes.process="*\\\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

CISA Adds Exploited SharePoint RCE Zero-Day CVE-2026-58644 to KEV

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 5 use cases 1 technique 6 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday added a newly patched security flaw impacting Microsoft SharePoint Server to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply the fixes by July 19, 2026. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-58644 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical deserialization

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SharePoint ToolPane.aspx exploitation POST with forged SignOut Referer (CVE-2026-58644)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell/LOLBin post-RCE (CVE-2026-58644) · [LLM] Webshell / DLL dropped in SharePoint LAYOUTS web path (spinstall0.aspx, CVE-2026-58644)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] IIS MachineKey / ValidationKey theft under w3wp lineage (CVE-2026-58644 post-exploit)
SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell/LOLBin post-RCE (CVE-2026-58644) AIInstallation High
Hunts for command interpreters and discovery LOLBins spawned as children of the SharePoint IIS worker process w3wp.exe. Successful exploitation of the CVE-2026-58644 deserialization RCE executes attacker code inside the w3wp context; a healthy SharePoint farm produces near-zero w3wp child processes, so any cmd/powershell/certutil/whoami/net child is high-signal. Rationale: w3wp.exe is the SharePoint/IIS worker; a legitimate farm virtually never spawns cmd/powershell/certutil children. CISA MAR-251132 and Microsoft's ToolShell reporting confirm this same family drops shells under w3wp — the parent+child pair is the article's RCE impact made concrete. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health analyzer jobs invoking stsadm or PowerShell during patch installation
  • Admins running Get-SPProduct / Config Wizard (psconfig) that shells out from an app-pool context during upgrades
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM/Nagios) that execute discovery commands under IIS identity
  • Legitimate custom web parts that shell out to cmd (rare, should be baselined and allowlisted)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig","stsadm -o","SPProductVersionTimerJob") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "OWSTIMER")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full process tree for the alerting w3wp child — capture ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, and the initiating account. Compare timing to any patch/psconfig maintenance window; genuine exploitation will show ad-hoc discovery (whoami/net) with no change ticket. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the SharePoint host from the network, kill the child process, and snapshot memory. Treat the farm as compromised — do NOT reboot before capturing artifacts. 3) HUNT: Search the same host for newly written .aspx files in LAYOUTS, command lines referencing MachineKey/ValidationKey (see companion UCs), and outbound connections from w3wp. Rotate IIS machine keys AFTER artifact removal per CISA guidance.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","bitsadmin.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","mshta.exe","reg.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\certutil.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\nltest.exe", @"\bitsadmin.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\reg.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SharePoint IIS Worker Process Spawning Shell or LOLBin (CVE-2026-58644)
id: 6b2f1c9a-3d4e-4a71-9f2c-8e1a7c0b5d21

  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-exploited-sharepoint-rce-zero.html
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations

  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003

Webshell / DLL dropped in SharePoint LAYOUTS web path (spinstall0.aspx, CVE-2026-58644) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of .aspx/.ashx/.asax/.dll files in SharePoint web-accessible directories (TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS, wss\VirtualDirectories, ISAPI) by w3wp.exe or a shell. Post-RCE the actor writes a webshell — publicly reported as spinstall0.aspx — into LAYOUTS to persist and to exfiltrate the IIS machine keys. Rationale: The SharePoint LAYOUTS/ISAPI/VirtualDirectories paths are web-reachable; a new .aspx there written by w3wp is the textbook ToolShell webshell drop. Filename spinstall0.aspx and these directories are corroborated in CISA MAR-251132 and Microsoft's ToolShell blog for this exact machine-key-theft chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint cumulative update / psconfig deploying new solution (.wsp) files that stage .aspx and .dll into LAYOUTS
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in installation (msiexec/SPSolution deploy) writing signed DLLs
  • Developer publishing a custom web part to a farm during a change window
  • Antivirus quarantine-and-restore cycling files in web directories
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","psconfig.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SolutionDeployment","install-spsolution",".wsp"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve the dropped file's SHA256 and contents; a genuine webshell will reference Request/Response, eval, or MachineKey/ValidationKey extraction. Confirm the writer was w3wp.exe with no matching solution-deploy change ticket. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, preserve the file (copy, don't delete), and block the source IP at the perimeter. Per CISA, remove intrusion artifacts BEFORE rotating machine keys. 3) HUNT: Grep IIS logs for GET/POST to the dropped filename to find operator IPs, pivot to any process reading web.config machine keys, and enumerate all farm servers for the same filename — the webshell is often deployed farm-wide.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Web Server Extensions\15\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\Web Server Extensions\16\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\inetpub\wwwroot\wss\VirtualDirectories", @"\Web Server Extensions\15\ISAPI", @"\Web Server Extensions\16\ISAPI")

IIS MachineKey / ValidationKey theft under w3wp lineage (CVE-2026-58644 post-exploit) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects processes descending from the SharePoint worker w3wp.exe whose command line references IIS cryptographic secrets (MachineKey, ValidationKey, DecryptionKey, Get-SPMachineKey). CISA explicitly calls out stealing IIS machine keys as the CVE-2026-58644 post-exploitation objective, enabling forged-ViewState persistent access even after patching. Rationale: CISA names 'stealing IIS machine keys' as the specific CVE-2026-58644 post-exploitation goal; ValidationKey/DecryptionKey/MachineKey are the exact strings the spinstall0.aspx shell extracts. Anchoring the keyword match to w3wp lineage separates attacker harvesting from routine admin key rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations • https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/sharepoint-toolshell-zero-day-exploited-in-the-wild-targets-enterprise-servers/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint admin manually rotating machine keys via Update-SPMachineKey / Set-SPMachineKey after the CISA advisory
  • Farm build automation that sets a consistent machineKey across web front-ends
  • Security team running validation scripts to inventory machine keys during IR
  • Config-management tooling (DSC/Ansible) templating web.config machineKey sections
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("sp_farm","svc-spadmin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Set-SPMachineKey","Update-SPMachineKey"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the invoking account is a known SharePoint farm admin and whether an approved key-rotation/IR task explains it. Attacker activity is spawned from w3wp with no interactive admin session. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, treat the machine keys as compromised — isolate the host, and plan a coordinated ValidationKey/DecryptionKey rotation across ALL farm servers (after removing webshells, per CISA order of operations). 3) HUNT: Correlate with UC2 (webshell drop) and IIS logs for forged-ViewState POSTs; forged machine keys grant persistent access indistinguishable from legit traffic, so review authentication anomalies going forward.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","MachineKey","Get-SPMachineKey","MachineKeySection","System.Web.Configuration.MachineKeySection")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","MachineKey","Get-SPMachineKey","MachineKeySection")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 9d3c2f18-4b6a-4e51-a72d-1c8f5b0e7a94
description: Detects command lines referencing IIS machine key material spawned under the SharePoint worker process, matching the CVE-2026-58644 machine-key harvesting post-exploitation step described by CISA.
references:

SharePoint ToolPane.aspx exploitation POST with forged SignOut Referer (CVE-2026-58644) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the network-facing exploitation signature of the CVE-2026-58644 chain in IIS access logs: an unauthenticated POST to /_layouts/*/ToolPane.aspx carrying a forged Referer of /_layouts/SignOut.aspx used to bypass authentication before the deserialization RCE. This targets the initial_access step directly on the wire. Rationale: The POST-to-ToolPane.aspx with a Referer forged to /_layouts/SignOut.aspx is the documented ToolShell auth-bypass signature CISA/Microsoft tie to this exact SharePoint machine-key-theft chain; it is a pre-auth network artifact with essentially no benign equivalent. Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty as IIS URI+Referer telemetry is not in those data sets in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit • https://www.forescout.com/blog/threat-analysis-microsoft-sharepoint-toolshell-exploits/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint page authoring that genuinely POSTs to ToolPane.aspx (Referer will NOT be SignOut.aspx, so the combined condition largely excludes this)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) replaying the ToolShell PoC during authorized testing
  • Security team validation of the patch using the public exploit
  • Load balancer / reverse proxy rewriting Referer headers in a way that coincidentally matches (rare)
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Tenable")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Record the source cIP, User-Agent, and scStatus. A 200/302 on this request indicates likely successful bypass; correlate the same cIP for follow-on GETs to newly created .aspx files. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter and, if a 2xx was returned, isolate the SharePoint server and treat the farm as compromised. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP across all farm front-ends, then jump to UC1/UC2/UC3 to confirm w3wp child processes, webshell drops, and machine-key theft on the targeted host. Verify AMSI integration is enabled per CISA hardening.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "/ToolPane.aspx"
| where csReferer has "/_layouts/SignOut.aspx"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-16 12 use cases 12 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

From late April 2026 to mid-June 2026, Microsoft Defender Experts observed increased ACR Stealer activity across customer environments. These campaigns are successfully using ClickFix lures to steal browser credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents from enterprise environments. The post ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Exposed Pheditor admin editor (pheditor.php) reachable over HTTP · [LLM] Repeated authentication POSTs to Pheditor (default-credential guessing / spray)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Pheditor terminal RCE invocation via HTTP (action=terminal / command=) · [LLM] Web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (Pheditor terminal RCE on host)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Web-server/PHP process writing new PHP webshell to web root · [LLM] Modification of Pheditor source file (pheditor.php) — hardcoded hash tamper · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-55579: Pheditor: Hardcoded default password 'admin' w
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Exposed Pheditor admin editor (pheditor.php) reachable over HTTP AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces any web request to pheditor.php, the single-file admin editor that ships with the hardcoded default password 'admin' (CVE-2026-55579). Because there is no forced password change, any internet-reachable pheditor.php is effectively an unauthenticated RCE endpoint, so simply locating exposed instances is the highest-leverage first pivot. Rationale: Keys on the literal endpoint path pheditor.php confirmed in the advisory and in the live repo source. Defender AH has no web-access-log table so defender_kql is empty; on Apache/nginx front ends substitute CommonSecurityLog.RequestURL for W3CIISLog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php • https://osv.dev/list
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer/sysadmin using Pheditor as an intended file editor
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing for pheditor.php
  • Uptime/monitoring checks hitting the admin path
  • Search-engine or asset-inventory crawlers indexing the web root
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host actually serves pheditor.php and whether it is internet-reachable; check the source IPs and user-agents hitting it for scanner vs. human patterns. Step 2 (contain): If exposed to untrusted networks, block the path at the WAF/reverse proxy, take the editor offline, and change the admin password off the default. Step 3 (hunt): Review UC for POST volume (spray), action=terminal requests, php spawning shells, and newly-written .php files on the same host to establish whether default creds were already used.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php"

Repeated authentication POSTs to Pheditor (default-credential guessing / spray) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a source IP sending many POST requests to pheditor.php in a short window — the shape of default-credential guessing against an instance that ships with password 'admin' and enforces no lockout, expiry, or forced change (CVE-2026-55579). Note: Pheditor returns HTTP 200 for BOTH success and failure, so this pivots on request volume rather than status code. Rationale: Because the app returns 200 on both correct and incorrect passwords (body 'The entry password is not correct.' on failure), a status-code 401->200 rule cannot work here; volume of POSTs to the single login endpoint is the reliable brute/spray signal. Threshold is commented and tunable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin repeatedly re-saving files (each POST hits pheditor.php)
  • Automated CI/CD or backup script interacting with the editor
  • A misconfigured session causing repeated re-login prompts
  • Load-balancer health checks POSTing to the app root
Suppression filter
| search NOT src IN ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the offending source IP's full request sequence; distinguish an admin doing many file saves (varied actions) from monotonic login attempts (repeated pheditor_password submissions). Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the WAF, force the admin password off 'admin', and invalidate active sessions. Step 3 (hunt): If any request in the burst was followed by action=terminal or upload-file activity, treat as compromise and pivot to endpoint UCs (php spawning shell / webshell writes).

| summarize Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName
| where Attempts >= 10   // 10 = single-user admin editor should see one login POST per session; 10 POSTs/hr from one IP is abnormal
| order by Attempts desc

| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 10
| sort - count
Pheditor terminal RCE invocation via HTTP (action=terminal / command=) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to pheditor.php carrying the terminal action and command parameter — the built-in terminal feature that yields immediate RCE once the default 'admin' password is used (CVE-2026-55579, and the related command-sanitization bypass CVE-2026-55578). Requires a WAF/proxy that logs query string and/or request body. Rationale: action=terminal and the command parameter are the exact terminal-feature strings confirmed from the Pheditor source. These params are POST body so detection requires WAF/proxy body or query logging; pair with the endpoint UC (php spawning shell) for confirmation where body capture is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using the Pheditor terminal for routine server tasks
  • Internal automation invoking the terminal action
  • Security testers validating the CVE in a sanctioned pentest
  • WAF false-parsing another app's 'command=' parameter (scope by pheditor.php path mitigates)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the decoded command string from RequestContext/body and the source IP; determine if the caller is a known admin from an expected network. Step 2 (contain): If unrecognized, isolate the web host, kill live php/shell child processes, block the source IP, and rotate the admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to endpoint telemetry for php->sh/bash execution and any newly-dropped .php files; review outbound connections from the web-server user for C2 or data staging.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has "pheditor.php"
| where RequestURL has "action=terminal" or RequestContext has "action=terminal" or RequestURL has "command=" or RequestContext has "command="
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (Pheditor terminal RCE on host) AIExploitation High
Highest-fidelity confirmation of Pheditor terminal RCE: a PHP interpreter or web-server process (php, php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2/httpd, w3wp) spawning an interactive shell or recon binary under the web-server account. This is the on-host footprint of the action=terminal command execution described in CVE-2026-55579 / CVE-2026-55578. Rationale: A file-editor's web process spawning /bin/sh + recon commands under www-data/apache is the deterministic on-host signature of the pheditor terminal feature; parent set covers php-fpm, mod_php (apache2/httpd) and IIS FastCGI (php-cgi.exe under w3wp). Datadog covers the Windows FastCGI case; Linux auditd lacks a clean parent field. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A PHP application legitimately shelling out (image thumbnailing via ImageMagick, git hooks, cron wrappers)
  • Deployment scripts run as the web-server user
  • Monitoring agents executing whoami/uname under the app account
  • Composer/artisan style tooling invoked by php-fpm
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","ffmpeg","git ","composer"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child process command line and full process tree; benign PHP shell-outs are narrow (e.g. convert, git), whereas RCE shows id/whoami/curl or an interactive shell. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, suspend the php-fpm/apache worker, capture volatile memory, and block any C2 IPs seen from the web account. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate .php/.phtml files written by the web process (webshell drop), review pheditor.php modification time, and correlate with inbound action=terminal requests in web/WAF logs.

| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server/PHP process writing new PHP webshell to web root AIInstallation Medium
Detects a PHP/web-server process creating a new .php/.phtml/.phar file — the on-host result of abusing Pheditor's file-upload (action=upload-file) or file-write editor features to drop a webshell after authenticating with the default password (CVE-2026-55579). Excludes pheditor.php itself (covered separately). Rationale: Pheditor's upload-file action and file editor let an authenticated (default-cred) attacker write arbitrary files; a web process creating new executable PHP content in the web root is the classic webshell-drop signature. Self-file pheditor.php excluded to route those to the dedicated modification UC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate deployments/CMS updates writing PHP cache or compiled templates (Twig/Blade cache) under the web user
  • Composer installing PHP packages into the web root
  • A developer legitimately using Pheditor to create new PHP files
  • Plugin/theme installers extracting .php archives
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "cache" and FolderPath !has "vendor" and FolderPath !has "storage/framework"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the newly-written file — template/cache artifacts are auto-generated and predictable, whereas a webshell contains eval/system/base64_decode/assert or request-parameter passthrough. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate the Pheditor admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Search web/WAF logs for subsequent GET/POST requests to the new file path, and check for php spawning shells and outbound C2 from the web account.

| where TargetFileName !endswith "pheditor.php"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Modification of Pheditor source file (pheditor.php) — hardcoded hash tamper AIInstallation Medium
Monitors writes/renames to pheditor.php itself. The advisory notes the SHA-512 default-password hash is stored at pheditor.php:11 and the in-app password change rewrites the hash directly into the source file — so any modification is either a legitimate credential change, a hardening action, or attacker persistence editing the admin hash. Flags changes lacking a change-control ticket. Rationale: The advisory explicitly states the SHA-512 hash lives at pheditor.php:11 and the password-change feature writes the new hash back into the source file; FIM on this exact filename catches both legitimate hardening (default hash replaced) and malicious hash swaps for persistent admin access. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1554 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin changing the Pheditor password via the app (rewrites the hash by design)
  • Scheduled deployment/git pull updating the file to a patched version (2.0.6+)
  • Sysadmin manually editing the file to remove the default hash (hardening)
  • Backup/restore operations touching the web root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and user — an in-app change is written by php-fpm/apache, whereas an editor (vim/nano/notepad) or unexpected account is worth scrutiny; confirm against change-control records. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, capture the pre-change hash from backups, restore a known-good pheditor.php, and force a fresh non-default password. Step 3 (hunt): Diff the modified file for an injected/attacker-controlled hash or added PHP, and correlate with prior action=terminal / webshell activity on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
